query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating the tungsten phase in a W–Cu composite with a thin nickel layer will suppress phase separation and inhibit interfacial void formation under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions, thereby improving the composite’s effective thermal conductivity relative to untreated composites.
generation.material_initial_state: W–Cu composite comprising tungsten particles or an interconnected tungsten ligament network embedded in a copper matrix.
generation.intervention: Apply an ultrathin nickel coating (on the order of 50–100 nm) onto the tungsten particles/ligaments prior to consolidation and joint fabrication.
generation.conditions: Processing and testing under heat-transfer and irradiation regimes relevant to plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling joints; for example, thermal exposures up to approximately 1000 °C and irradiation fluxes typical of fusion reactor wall conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The Ni coating is expected to improve interfacial wettability and reduce interfacial energy, thereby promoting a more coherent bond between tungsten and copper while acting as a diffusion barrier to suppress phase separation and mitigate void nucleation.
generation.mechanism: By enhancing wetting and bonding at the W–Cu interface, the nickel layer minimizes thermodynamically driven compositional segregation between tungsten and copper during high-temperature service. Additionally, the Ni interlayer limits irradiative defect accumulation and provides a barrier to void formation, thus sustaining an improved thermal path across the interface.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to an uncoated baseline composite, the nickel-coated composite is expected to exhibit a statistically significant increase in effective thermal conductivity (due to reduced interfacial resistance) and a lower density of interfacial voids upon exposure to the specified thermal and irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: W–Cu composite with unmodified tungsten phases (no interfacial coating) fabricated under identical processing conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated within the processing and service temperature range up to ~1000 °C and under moderate irradiation fluences typical of plasma-facing component joints. The intervention may not be effective under extreme conditions (e.g., temperatures significantly above 1000 °C or ultra-high irradiation doses) beyond those anticipated in the target application.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal Ni coating thickness and long-term stability under cyclic irradiation and thermal cycling remain to be fully determined. It is also uncertain whether the Ni interlayer might introduce any secondary phase issues over extended service times.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set with tungsten particles/ligaments pre-coated with a 50–100 nm Ni layer and another set with uncoated tungsten, fabricated under identical conditions. Subject both sets to accelerated thermal cycling and irradiation tests replicating the operational conditions of joints between plasma-facing materials and Cu-cooled components. In situ and post-test analyses will be conducted.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of effective thermal conductivity (e.g., via laser flash analysis) before and after testing.
Microscopic evaluation (electron microscopy, tomography) of the interfacial regions to quantify void density and assess phase separation.
Interfacial bonding quality assessment using techniques such as TEM or SIMS.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nickel-coated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in effective thermal conductivity and a reduction in interfacial void density relative to the uncoated baseline, then the hypothesis will be rejected.
